articles.text: In partial returns late last night, Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson have commanding leads in the race for two open seats on the Piedmont School Board. At 8:36 p.m., approximately 1,700 ballots had been cast in the school board and city council election. The city has a total of 8,804 registered voters. At approximately 11 p.m. Tuesday night, Medhekar is the leading vote getter with 41.39% of the vote, and Thomasson was at 39.62%. Shirley Hooi trailed Thomasson by roughly 20% of the vote. “The campaign was a great experience. I got to meet and talk with so many people around town, which made me feel even more connected to our community,” said Medhekar. “I am grateful for the confidence the voters have shown in me tonight, and most importantly, I am excited to get to work on the school board to help foster positive dialogue and advocate for a high-quality and nurturing school experience for our kids.” There are no incumbents in this race, and all three candidates were first-time candidates. “The campaign has been challenging yet incredibly informative,” said Thomasson. “Tonight I am grateful for each constituent who came out to speak with me, share their perspectives, insights, and experience. Now we get to work. The challenges are significant and yet I am confident that we have the knowledge and determination in this community to come together and solve them,” said Thomasson. articles.text: The following is an abridged version of a letter sent to Piedmont City Council on November 6 by residents on Oakland Avenue. Editor: As Piedmont residents directly affected by the new plans for the Oakland Avenue Bulb-Out at Jerome Avenue we are writing to protest and object to certain aspects of the new plans. The new plans include for the first time the removal and relocation of two long existing AC Transit Bus stops at the corners of Oakland Avenue and Jerome Avenue and Oakland Avenue and Latham Street and the loss of at least 4 parking spaces that are used every day by residents. The new plans differ in material and substantial ways from the Bulb-Out and flashing Lights plans and proposals previously presented in City Staff reports and in the plain language of the City Council minutes and resolutions on which residents relied for their information. Many of the signatories to this Notice are long-time residents of the local area, and some of us have lived here for over 45 years. We are fully cognizant of the AC Transit bus traffic patterns and bus stops in our area, as many of us have for decades used the buses running up and down Oakland Avenue. We are also very familiar with the vehicular traffic patterns and parking needs on Oakland and Jerome Avenues and Latham Steet. We are approaching these new City proposed traffic measures not as idealogues but as practical people and residents who know what is going on in our neighborhood. At no time prior to the revelation of the current plans on October 29, 2022, were residents informed of the removal of the bus stops and parking or the relocation of bus stops, nor does it appear that this proposed radical change in the plans was discussed in public or addressed in staff reports or in open City Council meetings. The April 15, 2019 Piedmont Council Agenda Report contained a recommendation submitted by Public Works Director Chester Nakahara to the Mayor and City Council regarding “Review of Preliminary Designs for Traffic Calming Measures at Oakland Ave. at El Cerrito Ave. and Oakland Ave. at Jerome Ave. ”The recommendation attached a plan and commented that the 4 corner bulbout design would include rapid flashing beacons, new pedestrian ramps and refreshed street paint. The recommendation never mentioned, nor did the attached plan show, removal or relocation of bus stops or the abolition of at least 4 parking spaces. The October 5, 2020 Piedmont Council Agenda Report authored by Mr. Nakahara noted that the City Engineer would be bringing the Oakland Ave. BulbOuts Project to the City Council for review and discussion soon. Exhibit A to that Agenda stated with respect to the Oakland Ave. Bulb-Outs Project that the Preliminary Designs were completed as of 9/28/2020 and the next steps would require Council direction on design iterations. Once again there was no mention of removing or relocating bus stops or removing 4 parking spaces. articles.text: November 1 was All Saints Day on the Christian calendar. While not every Christian church, or every Christian denomination, observes All Saints Day, for many it is an essential expression of their faith. As Professor Sarah Birmingham Drummond notes, “Most communities of faith that mark All Saints Day focus their attention on remembering those in the church who have died in the previous year. Such celebrations provide comfort to those who are still in mourning by reminding them that, in spirit, the loved ones are still present, particularly in the context of Christian worship.” One of the scripture readings for All Saints is Ephesians 1:11- 23. In this letter the writer, by tradition Paul, address the people as saints, praises their faith, urges them to respect what God is doing in and through them and encourages them to realize that as saints, as holy ones, they are part of the ongoing saga of resurrection; part of the amazing story of God making a broken world whole. The New Revised Standard Version of the Bible puts it this way: May you know the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance among the saints (v18). The words of Ephesians are elevated, encouraging, even soaring. To be a saint is to be part of a community with past, present and future dimensions that is entrusted with the mission of expressing the hope of God in every time and every place. Colleague George Mason, who recently retired as pastor of Wilshire Baptist Church in Dallas, Texas, adds some needed context to our understanding of living as saints, of honoring the saints that have gone before and of expressing God’s hope. He notes that there are some who would have us think that to fulfill our “saintliness” we must strive do exactly what the first followers of Jesus, such as Paul and the Ephesians, did. He does not believe we can do this. “We don’t disregard the early church’s decisions; we reckon with them. They could not foresee every circumstance in ages to come,” he writes. Rather than trying to do exactly what the saints of old did, he urges us to do as they did, discerning the way of hope anew and making decisions under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. I find this

articles.text: Staff photo Resident and architect Chuck Oraftik measures driveways at Oakland and Jerome Aves. to compare with city bulb-out plans. A year ago, on October 4, 2021, Piedmont City Council first approved design plans for the construction of bulb-outs on Oakland Avenue at the intersections of El Cerrito Avenue and Jerome Avenue. At an on-site meeting on November 1 a week ago, as directed by the city staff, the plans were shared with neighbors. The proposals were based upon the Piedmont Safer Streets Plan, adopted in December 2021, which listed the Jerome and El Cerrito intersections as among the 10 high priority crossings for pedestrian safety improvements. The current plan calls for four permanent “bulb-outs” at each intersection where the sidewalk extends and the street shrinks, to make the pedestrian crossing shorter and safer. In addition to the bulb-outs, the plan provides for high-visibility crosswalks, pedestrian ramps, yellow flashing beacons, new street paint, and new signs at each intersection. Despite the public engagement plan prescribed by the Piedmont Safer Streets Plan, however, the bulb-out proposal has received low support from those it affects. Residents overwhelmingly agree with the need for slower traffic on Oakland Avenue, as is reflected in community surveys by city staff. Oakland Avenue residents Jonah Levy and Helga Ying, as example, have called for more pedestrian safety measures like speed bumps, signage, and bicycle infrastructure. However, many neighbors of the targeted intersections on Oakland Ave. feel that they have been hastily and scantily informed of some of the consequences – the elimination of 10 street parking spots and the relocation of four bus stops. As one resident explained, “Our community doesn’t call it the bulb-out problem, we call it the bus stop problem.” The intention behind the bulb-out plan — pedestrian safety on the busiest street in Piedmont — may present little problem. Residents initially saw a benefit to the installation of bollards at the intersection on Greenbank Avenue in April 2019. But a better solution was found” installing two newly designed speed bumps on the narrow street. Bollards, one resident said, “is like putting a Band-Aid on a wound.” Another resident, perusing weeks of City Council meetings regarding the bulb-outs, found nothing about bus stops; nor are buses mentioned in the Piedmont Safer Streets plan, except for a statement ensuring that “neighborhood traffic calming measures do not negatively impact [bus] access.” Some of the existing crosswalks along these intersections already empty onto private driveways. Given that the impacted homes will lose parking spots, many residents contend that the bulb-out plan will create more pedestrian traffic, not less, on a busy street. Nor is there a precedent for this parking spot displacement, given that the other bus stops along Oakland Avenue are placed in deliberately non-invasive areas — where houses don’t face the street, and nearly always along a shrub wall. Oakland Avenue residents are hoping the City can describe how the current plan benefits those it will directly affect. business hours.

articles.text: The Piedmont Post has begun its 25th year of publishing the community’s weekly newspaper. It’s first edition was on October 20, 1998, a 12-page paper that hardly offered any promise, let alone optimism, that it might be around a quarter century later. In a small town with only a few commercial businesses, the outlook for its survival was somewhat bleak. Ten years later we began reading stories in the New York Times about the large number of local newspapers going out of business – over 2,000 at last count. And yet here we are – thriving and finding ways to thank the residents for so strongly supporting The Little Newspaper That Could. During the next several weeks and months, you will read comments of some of the people who were there at the beginning – the optimists and pragmatists.
articles.title: 25th Anniversary of Piedmont Post

articles.text: Editor: How is it possible that the Post is already 25 years old? Very few would have taken up the challenge of starting a serious, subscription-based newspaper in a small town. Too many chances to fail. But the Post has survived and flourished. From the beginning, it has covered stories often overlooked by the large regional papers but important to our multi-generational community (and especially to the parents of school-age children!). in a well-written, evenhanded manner, and – where appropriate – a self-deprecating sense of humor Hats off to the Post, our hometown paper. –Rick Eigenbrode and Pat Nicholas, Palm Drive

The proposals were based upon the Piedmont Safer Streets Plan, adopted in December 2021, which listed the Jerome and El Cerrito intersections as among the 10 high priority crossings for pedestrian safety improvements. The current plan calls for four permanent “bulb-outs” at each intersection where the sidewalk extends and the street shrinks, to make the pedestrian crossing shorter and safer. In addition to the bulb-outs, the plan provides for high-visibility crosswalks, pedestrian ramps, yellow flashing beacons, new street paint, and new signs at each intersection. Despite the public engagement plan prescribed by the Piedmont Safer Streets Plan, however, the bulb-out proposal has received low support from those it affects. Residents overwhelmingly agree with the need for slower traffic on Oakland Avenue, as is reflected in community surveys by city staff. Oakland Avenue residents Jonah Levy and Helga Ying, as example, have called for more pedestrian safety measures like speed bumps, signage, and bicycle infrastructure. However, many neighbors of the targeted intersections on Oakland Ave. feel that they have been hastily and scantily informed of some of the consequences – the elimination of 10 street parking spots and the relocation of four bus stops. As one resident explained, “Our community doesn’t call it the bulb-out problem, we call it the bus stop problem.” The intention behind the bulb-out plan — pedestrian safety on the busiest street in Piedmont — may present little problem. Residents initially saw a benefit to the installation of bollards at the intersection on Greenbank Avenue in April 2019. But a better solution was found” installing two newly designed speed bumps on the narrow street. Bollards, one resident said, “is like putting a Band-Aid on a wound.” Another resident, perusing weeks of City Council meetings regarding the bulb-outs, found nothing about bus stops; nor are buses mentioned in the Piedmont Safer Streets plan, except for a statement ensuring that “neighborhood traffic calming measures do not negatively impact [bus] access.” Some of the existing crosswalks along these intersections already empty onto private driveways. Given that the impacted homes will lose parking spots, many residents contend that the bulb-out plan will create more pedestrian traffic, not less, on a busy street. Nor is there a precedent for this parking spot displacement, given that the other bus stops along Oakland Avenue are placed in deliberately non-invasive areas — where houses don’t face the street, and nearly always along a shrub wall. Oakland Avenue residents are hoping the City can describe how the current plan benefits those it will directly affect. articles.text: Healthy donors needed to give now The American Red Cross urges blood and platelet donors to give now and help fight the potential impact of seasonal illnesses and a potentially severe flu season on the blood supply. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention predicts a serious spread of flu this year and is already reporting an early spike in cases in several states. When seasonal illnesses increase, the number of healthy donors tends to decrease, leaving the Red Cross blood supply vulnerable to a potential shortage over the holidays. Paired with busy holiday schedules, seasonal illnesses may make it harder to collect the blood hospital patients require this winter. Donors − especially those with type O blood and those giving platelets − can help bolster the blood supply now by making an appointment to give in the coming weeks. There is no waiting period to donate blood or platelets after receiving a flu shot. Schedule an appointment by using the Red Cross Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood.org or calling 1-800-RED CROSS (1-800-733- 2767). As thanks, the Red Cross is offering several opportunities to donors this month: • Everyone who donates until November 22 will receive a $10 e-gift card to a merchant of choice. Details are available at rcblood.org/perks. • Those donating who come to give over the Thanksgiving holiday, November 23-27, will get a Red Cross knit beanie, while supplies last. Details are available at rcblood.org/together. For more infromation, call the Oakland Blood Bank at 6230 Claremont Avenue. Tel. (510) 594-5210.

articles.text: NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that at 5:30 p.m. on November 14, 2022, the Planning Commission will review an ordinance amending Chapter 17 (Planning and Land Use) of the City Code to conform the City’s regulations regarding Accessory Dwelling Units to new state laws and make a recommendation to the City Council. The ordinance also includes a new division 17.42 to address CA Assembly Bill 916, which requires ministerial review for the development of new bedrooms within existing residential units. NOTICE IS FURTHER GIVEN that at 6:00 p.m. on November 21, 2022, the City Council will consider the proposed ordinance and the recommendation of the Planning Commission and could approve the first reading of the ordinance. Background On January 1, 2022, new state laws come into effect which further limit a local jurisdiction’s ability to regulate Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs). The provisions affected by the changes to state law include but are not limited to: street (front) yard setbacks, unit height limitations, approval of existing conditions inconsistent with current Building Code requirements, interior connections between a Junior Accessory Dwelling Unit and the Primary Dwelling Unit, and the separate conveyance of ADUs. City staff is also recommending an incentive for the development of affordable ADUs in exchange for the release of owner-occupancy restrictions. Local laws which do not conform to these new state standards are preempted and cannot be enforced. The ordinance also proposes a new City Code division 17.42 that establishes a ministerial review process for projects that develop no more than two additional bedrooms within an existing dwelling unit, in conformance with AB 916 (2022). City staff has developed the proposed ordinance which will be considered by the Planning Commission and the City Council to conform Piedmont’s ADU regulations to the new state law. Documents on the City Website Documents related to this effort are available on the City website at piedmont.ca.gov. A staff report to the Planning Commission dated November 14, 2022, is provided on the website. It includes the proposed changes that will bring the City’s regulations for ADUs and additional bedrooms into compliance with the new state laws. The Planning Commission’s responsibility is to make a recommendation for consideration by the City Council, which is the decision-making body. The City Council staff report for this item will be posted on the City website no later than 12 noon on Friday, November 18, 2022. Public Engagement The opportunity for public input is available throughout this process. Interested members of the public are encouraged to attend the public meetings. Both the Planning Commission meeting on November 14, 2022, and the City Council meeting on November 21, 2022, will be televised live on KCOM-TV, the City’s government access TV station and available through streaming video on the City’s web site at piedmont.ca.gov/. articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) student’s standardized test scores for the 2021-22 school year earned the district top three rankings in California. All public school districts are required to take the California Assessments of Student Performance and Progress (CAASPP) test, which tests subject matter, critical thinking, analytical writing, and problem-solving skills. The CAASPP is a collection of computer-based assessments in English Language literacy and Mathematics and Science. The CAASPP replaced the paperbased Standardized Testing and Reporting (STAR) program in 2014. Last spring, Piedmont students in grades 3–8, and grade 11 participated in the 2021-22 CAASPP for English Language Arts (ELA) and Math. Students in grades 5, 8, and 12, participated in a Science test. The California Department of Education released school, district and state aggregate results on October 24. Piedmont students demonstrated a high level of achievement overall on the CAASPP, ranking second among California unified school districts in English Language Arts and third in Math. Overall, more than 87% of Piedmont students met or exceeded state standards in English, marking a 2% increase from 2021, as well as a return to the district’s pre-pandemic score. In Mathematics, 81% of students met or exceeded state standards, 5.5% below pre-pandemic levels. In Science, nearly 75% of PUSD students met or exceeded state standards. To see Piedmont’s full test results visit Tinyurl.com/pusdcaaspp2022 for ELA and Math, and Tinyurl.com/ pusdcast2022 for Science. State results show that approximately 47% of students met or exceeded standards in English Language Arts (down four points from 2019), 33% in Math (down seven points), and 29% in Science (down one one point). “This is exciting news from the state and another wonderful testament to the hard work of Piedmont students, teachers and staff,” said Interim School Superintendent, Dr. Donald Evans. “To show such resiliency in reaching or approaching the District’s preCOVID results, despite everything they’ve gone through, demonstrates students’ willingness to learn and educators’ dedication to supporting them in every way.” The CAASPP assessments are one gauge of student progress, providing information to schools, teachers, and parents about how students perform relative to California’s goals for both learning and college and career readiness. The results will be used as one of several means to determine and meet student needs and guide discussions among parents and teachers. Individual scores were made available in the fall and can be seen online on the Infinite Campus Parent Portal. Directions are available on the district website.

pages.text: 6 Wednesday, November 9, 2022 SchOOLs By Jay Russell Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) student’s standardized test scores for the 2021-22 school year earned the district top three rankings in California. All public school districts are required to take the California Test results for top public school districts in state ENG MATH La Canada Unified, Flintridge 87.9% San Marino Unified 83.3% Piedmont Unified 87.1% La Canada Unified 83.2% San Marino Unified 87.0% Piedmont Unified 81.0% Palo Alto Unified 83.1% Sunol Glen Unified 79.9% Manhattan Beach Unified 82.0% Palo Alto Unified 78.9% Oak Park Unified, Thousand Oaks 81.2% South Pasadena Unified 75.4% Dublin Unified 81.0% Dublin Unified 74.2% South Pasadena Unified 80.6% Pleasanton Unified 73.6% Palos Verdes Peninsula Unified 80.4% Manhattan Beach Unified 73.2% San Ramon Valley 79.7% Palos Verdes Peninsula Unified 72.8% Resources for families • Visit Greatschools.org/gk/test-guide for a detailed explanation of test results for each grade level and subject. • CAASPP tests, sample reports, and help for families: Test Score Guide website “Starting Smarter” Ca.startingsmarter.org • Complete Sample Individual Score Report Caaspp.org/administration/reporting/student-score-report.html Piedmont school district ranks in top 3 on state tests Assessments of Student Performance and Progress (CAASPP) test, which tests subject matter, critical thinking, analytical writing, and problem-solving skills. The CAASPP is a collection of computer-based assessments in English Language literacy and Mathematics and Science. The CAASPP replaced the paperbased Standardized Testing and Reporting (STAR) program in 2014. Last spring, Piedmont students in grades 3–8, and grade 11 participated in the 2021-22 CAASPP for English Language Arts (ELA) and Math. Students in grades 5, 8, and 12, participated in a Science test. The California Department of Education released school, district and state aggregate results on October 24. Piedmont students demonstrated a high level of achievement overall on the CAASPP, ranking second among California unified school districts in English Language Arts and third in Math. Overall, more than 87% of Piedmont students met or exceeded state standards in English, marking a 2% increase from 2021, as well as a return to the district’s pre-pandemic score. In Mathematics, 81% of students met or exceeded state standards, 5.5% below pre-pandemic levels. In Science, nearly 75% of PUSD students met or exceeded state standards. To see Piedmont’s full test results visit Tinyurl.com/pusdcaaspp2022 for ELA and Math, and Tinyurl.com/ pusdcast2022 for Science. State results show that approximately 47% of students met or exceeded standards in English Language Arts (down four points from 2019), 33% in Math (down seven points), and 29% in Science (down one one point). “This is exciting news from the state and another wonderful testament to the hard work of Piedmont students, teachers and staff,” said Interim School Superintendent, Dr. Donald Evans. “To show such resiliency in reaching or approaching the District’s preCOVID results, despite everything they’ve gone through, demonstrates students’ willingness to learn and educators’ dedication to supporting them in every way.” The CAASPP assessments are one gauge of student progress, providing information to schools, teachers, and parents about how students perform relative to California’s goals for both learning and college and career readiness. The results will be used as one of several means to determine and meet student needs and guide discussions among parents and teachers. Individual scores were made available in the fall and can be seen online on the Infinite Campus Parent Portal. Directions are available on the district website. articles.text: For over 30 years, Scouts have collected non-perishable food for the Alameda County Community Food Bank. The tradition continues this Saturday morning, November 12, when Piedmont Scouts will go door-to-door to pick of bags of non-perishable food being donated by residents, and which will be delivered to the Food Bank. Last year’s food drive generated more than 9,000 pounds of food and raised over $4,500 through the Scout virtual food drive. One week ago Piedmont residents received door hangers reminding them of the citywide food drive. Residents are encouraged to leave donations of nutritious, non-perishable food in recycled boxes or bags outside their doors before 9:00 a.m. this Saturday morning. Alameda County has one of the highest rates of hunger in the nation. One of every five Alameda County residents rely on the food bank for assistance, and two-thirds of those are children and the elderly. Help eliminate hunger by donating non-perishable foods such as: canned fruits, vegetables, and meats; canned soup; peanut butter; pasta and canned sauce. Troop 6 Scouts Charlie and JD Sellman shown last year with bags of donated food. Door hangers were left at residences throughout Piedmont last week reminding them that Saturday, November 12, is the annual Scouting for Food citywide campaign In addition, residents can participate in the virtual food drive by visiting the website (https:// donate.accf b.org/vfd/Member/ MyPage/5806787/Boy-Scoutsof-America?tab=MyPage), where $1 becomes 2 meals for children, adults, and seniors in the community. Help the Scouts reach their goal of $10,000. For more information contact Eris Turner at the Scout office at 510-844-4752. Visit the website www.piedmontbsa.org for additional information about the annual food collection program.

articles.text: Meeting scheduled for Nov. 16 at Alan Harvey Theater A public forum has been scheduled for residents to provide input in the Piedmont School Board’s search for a permanent school superintendent. The meeting will be held on Wednesday, November 16, at 6:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater. Residents will have an opportunity to interact with consultants from the search firm, Leadership Associates, which has been hired by the school board to lead the search. Residents are asked to provide input about desired personal and professional qualities anticipated in the incoming superintendent. Comment from the public will be used in the development of the candidate profile, recruitment process, and reference checking. The consultants from Leadership Associates will also compile a summary of all comments received during these sessions and share the report with the School Board and with the future superintendent. During the forum, consultants will share an overview of the process, and ask audience members the following questions: • What are the desirable qualities, characteristics, background and professional and personal experiences for the next superintendent? • What do you see as the strengths of the district and the major challenges facing the district in years ahead? There is no need to RSVP. If unable to attend, individuals will have an opportunity to provide feedback and responses to these questions on an online survey. The survey will activate on November 14 and remain open until November 21. For this year’s fall play, Piedmont High’s advanced acting class asked, “Is love a game?” with three performances of Jane Austin’s classic story, Pride and Prejudice. articles.text: Photos by Sohrab “Seb” Ford Children’s Fairyland Fairyland.org 699 Bellevue Avenue, Oakland, 452-2259 Fairyland is a mid-century 10-acre fantasy world for young children. The park has new puppet shows in its open-air Children’s Storybook Theater. Tam and Cam, a popular Cinderella tale from Vietnam is coming in November, along with the Lewis Carrol classic, Alice in Wonderland. Fairyland is open five days a week, Wednesday to Sunday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Lawrence Hall of Science Lawrencehallofscience.org 1 Centennial Drive, Berkeley 642-5132 The Hall is open for visitors to explore the wonders of science and the universe Wednesday–Sunday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. For more than 50 years the Hall has enabled kids to discover something new with hands-on exhibits for all ages. See Sunstones II, the 3-D theater and explore the Cambrian Explosion. Exploratorium Exploratorium.edu Pier 15, San Francisco (415) 528-4444 The Exploratorium has interactive exhibits that are outof-the-world and invite participation. You will be amazed at the dozens of exhibits ready for kids and parents. Among the mind-blowing exhibits are the Aeolian harps, anamorphic benches, the Bacteriopolis, and the chaotic pendulum. The Exploratorium has more exhibits, features and activities than can be seen in one day, so consider a membership. Open Wed.-Friday, 10 a.m.–5 p.m. Thursday nights for ages 18 & older from 6–10 p.m., and Sunday from 12 noon to 5 p.m. Academy of Science Calacademy.org Golden Gate Park, 55 Music Concourse Dr., S.F. (415) 379-8000 California Academy of Science in Golden Gate Park has a four-story rainforest with everything from butterflies to the bioluminescent depths of the “twilight zone.” The Academy’s newest exhibit, “Bugs”, was created by Te Papa Tongarewa Museum of New Zealand and Weta Workshop (the creative studio behind the Lord of the Rings films’ sets). It reveals the secrets of insects and arthropods in delightful, dazzling ways. The Academy is open Mon. to Saturday, 9:30 a.m.-5:00 p.m., Thursday night for ages 18 & older from 6 - 10 p.m., and Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. “We were really excited this year because we have a new theater. It opened up lots of new possibilities,” said Lorin. “Everyone just had a new level of excitement, which I think made this show better than usual.” The play, set in 19th century England, follows Elizabeth “Lizzy” Bennet and her sisters as they struggle in the game of love. The sisters encounter strict gender constructs, class conflict, and a persistent mother, Mrs. Bennet, set on marrying her four daughters off to the richest bachelors. Though Lizzy is insistent she will never marry, she ends up falling for Mr. Darcy. Lizzy navigates this dynamic switch while attempting to retain her strength of character. The play is “empowering but also hilarious,” commented Lorin adding that the story suggests “you can have a man, but still be a feminist.”

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. articles.text: Part 2 of Sally the Witch As the midnight wind blew through Sally’s hair, she looked down to see the lights of Salem glowing and twinkling beneath her. Flying over the magic district, Sally could see the old, empty building at the corner of Looking Glass Way, and breathed a heavy sigh. It had been her dream to own an enchanted bookstore ever since she was able to cast a spell – usually around two or three years old. (Witches and wizards are fast learners.) Sally figured her bookstore would be filled with texts of worlds long forgotten, spellbooks, and potion journals that had been in her family for hundreds of years. The store would even have books on enchanted cooking. Sally’s grandmother had owned a bookstore centuries ago, and as a young girl she would go with her mother to sit in a favorite corner by the fireplace. The bookstore was filled with soft lights of all colors and with plants from around the world. Sally would sit and read her favorite book, “The Tales of Agatha the Wise.” It was about the adventures of a witch who could wield the elements. Contrary to popular beliefs about witches, Agatha helped people. Sally always remembered the fireplace with green flames and the shelves with thousands of books. She also remembered the terrible day that the bookstore caught fire and burned down. The books were saved, but not the building, and since that day Sally had a dream of recreating her grandmother’s bookstore as her own. Out of the corner of her eye, Sally noticed a “For Sale” sign. She slammed the brakes on her broom, almost knocking Lucinda, her cat, out of the pet passenger seat. Whooshing down to Looking Glass Way, Sally jumped off her broom and ran to the building. But before we go on with Sally’s story, I must inform you that buying property as a magical being is a different process than for mere humans. Sally walked up to the building and began bargaining for the price. After many different offers both parties came to the agreement of 300 gold coins. A moderately cheap price, considering that there were curses on the building and it was inhabited by ghosts. But those were part of Sally’s everyday life. Nonetheless, Sally excitedly picked up the key, opened the door, and walked inside. The main floor was a big open space with gothic style windows and a fireplace. The floors were wooden and creaked when stepped on. The second level was reached by a spiral wooden staircase with ivy on the railing and steps, the level itself was a loft that included more gothic windows. Eager to create her dream store, Sally decided to start renovating that same day. She hopped onto her broom and flew home as fast as she could. Arriving at her cottage she put a charm that levitated anything that it was cast on, and she cast it on all of the books and some of the shelves to make it easier to transport them. As she flew through the early morning sky she looked behind her and started to laugh; s30 flying bookshelves and thousands of books following her. As she made it back to the bookstore the furniture and books followed her in. She started to arrange the bookshelves and the books began to find their designated sections and shelves. While the books and furniture were arranging themselves, Sally noticed that there were sofas tucked away in the back of the store. She put a Gemini charm on it and suddenly there six couches appeared. The bookstore was coming together, the books were exactly where they were supposed to be, the couches had been placed strategically near the windows and corners. Sally enchanted the ivy on the stairs to help decorate all the shelves and windowsills. Remembering her grandmother’s bookstore, she pulled a book off the shelves named “103 Ways to Light Up A Room, Literally.” The final thing she did was to light the fireplace with green flames. And just like that, The Bookstore On Looking Glass Way was open for business. Larissa Edel, a student at Bentley School, sent this story as a post-Halloween treat.

articles.text: Piedmont’s Fire and Police Departments held a Wildfire Evacuation Drill on Saturday morning, November 5, the first of its kind in the city. Despite some morning rain, participation was high in both the evacuation of residents in high risk-homes and the debriefing at Community Hall afterwards. Approximately 50 homes above Coaches Field (Maxwelton Road, Abbot Way, Echo Lane, Nellie Avenue) were identified as the area at the highest risk for wildfire due to the isolated locale and wooded surroundings. Historically, large wildfires in Oakland have come over the hill near the Piedmont border. “The police department was able to knock on every door in the evacuation neighborhood in about 45 minutes,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “I thought it was a great accomplishment. They were able to physically check on every single house in the area.” Brannigan mentioned that there were 615 downloads of the at-home fire-drill activities and over 1,000 visits for the fire evacuation exercise. During the drill Piedmont’s Public Works Department was called on to clear the Corporation Yard of critical equipment that might have been in harm’s way during an emergency and to redirect the equipment to firefighters at the top of the hill on Maxwelton Road. “The city staff that participated got a lot out of it. We did have some good lessons learned, and not everything went perfectly. We have some things to figure out and improve, and that’s the whole point [of the drill],” Brannigan added. articles.text: Both veteran and new Petal It Forward ambassadors gathered at J. Miller Flowers on Wednesday, October 19, to begin their 8th Annual Petal It Forward celebration – and what a celebration it was. Petal It Forward is a national program sponsored by the Society of American Florists that shares the emotional and healing power of flowers. There are more than 450 events in more than 400 cities in the U.S. and in Canada and India. In each country it is quite an undertaking. Quite simply, it is a random-acts-of-kindness event, with flowers as the focal point of interest for all involved. More than a dozen volunteers trimmed, assembled, and wrapped hundreds of bouquets with flowers donated by Santa Rose Wholesale, Pacific Coast Evergreen, Mt. Eden Floral, Neve Brothers, Torchio Nursery, Rafas Floral, and Repetto’s Nursery. Many growers have donated year after year, and their beautiful blooms are a huge part of what makes Petal It Forward such a meaningful day every year. Two bouquets are given to each recipient – one to keep, and one to give to someone else. The group’s first stop was UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital in Oakland. The flowers were barely unloaded and volunteers just fanning out when a mom arrived alone, her shoulder down and her heart in her throat. She was given two bouquets, and tears were shed by all as the mom told the groud her child came to Children’s a week ago as a trauma patient. It was clear by the pain on her face that this had been the hardest week of her life. She said that this small act of Gisele Rainier (left), Shari Santos, Stacey Hanover, Danielle Baca, Valerie Lee, and Bob Otsuka in front of UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital in Oakland. kindness was a beautiful, unexpected gesture in such a difficult time. Although she couldn’t take the flowers to her child’s room, she promised to take a picture and show her daughter how total strangers had given the bouquets to her and how appreciative she was. There were many moments like that, with worried parents receiving a moment of beauty when they were least expecting it but needing it most. Children were bringing the second bouquet to their grandparents or someone else important to them, and their pride at bringing flowers home brought smiles to all everyone’s faces. The group then brought flowers to Mountain Music on Piedmont Avenue, a store had recently robbed, and whose owners appreciated a bright spot in their day. They also brought flowers to the Piedmont Avenue Holistic Veterinarian and their office puppy. The last stops were Pizza Violetta, whose owner, Violetta’s dad Jonathan, had provided delicious pizzas to the hungry volunteers making bouquets the day before. Another wonderful visit was to the dedicated team across the street from the flower shop on Piedmont Avenue at Chapel of the Chimes. As is done every year, each volunteer is asked to share their favorite moment. More than one mentioned the first woman they met, whose tears reminded them how important Petal It Forward is, especially to those with sick or injured children. Another volunteer said that she loved how unexpected and appreciated every recipient found the small act of giving. Another said that Petal It Forward reminded them of how such a small act can bring such an emotional moment for someone who truly needs it. Valerie Lee, co-owner of J. Miller Flowers, said that one of her favorite reasons for putting in the extra hours and extra work year in and year out is that it’s for her community – as a person and as a member of the Piedmont, Oakland, and Contra Costa community. articles.text: Emma Eisemon, Cecilia DeFazio place 2nd in doubles Staff Photos Tanya Kononova won the WACC Tennis Singles title on November 5 with a victory over Alameda’s Juliana Johnson. Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team had a successful showing at the 2022 Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament at Chabot College last weekend, November 4-5. Firstyear student Tanya Kononova, a junior, won the singles championship, and the doubles team of junior Cecilia DeFazio and sophomore Emma Eisemon placed second. Kononova defeated Alameda’s Juliana Johnson on Saturday in straight sets 6-3, 7-5, and marked her third win of the season over Johnson. “I just waited until the moment I could make myself calm and in the mood where I could win. I didn’t want to play a third set because I was unsure if I could handle the pressure,” said Kononova, who arrived from Ukraine in late summer. But though But though seeded No. 1 in the tournament, she admitted she had some concerns. She had to fight through some frustrating moments in the second set to win 7-5, but was able to hammer home the win with her usual array of powerful serves, forehands, and backhands. For the final point, Johnson was unable to return a strong forehand by Kononova, forcing the Alameda starter to commit an error on an attempt that flew out of bounds. “It feels strange; I was so emotional today. It felt like was playing against myself. I just need to practice and gain more experience, because this match was good experience to gain. When I play in a similar situation, I’ll know that I’ve already been through a tough challenge and Emma Eisemon and Cecilia DeFazio (not pictured) finished second in the WACC doubles bracket. Michaela Bini (front) and Anne Jumper took third-place in the doubles ladder.

articles.text: After receiving a first-round bye, the No. 3 seeded Piedmont High boys’ water polo team defeated No. 6 Novato in the Division 2 North Coast Section quarterfinals on Saturday, November 5 at Amador Valley in Pleasanton. PHS advances to the semifinals and will face No. 2 Marin Academy today, Wednesday, November 9 in San Rafael. “It was kind of a shootout. We were scoring goals and Novato was scoring goals. We had a really balanced attack. Everybody was involved and that’s what really carried us through the game. It wasn’t our best defensive effort. It was our balanced scoring attack that got it done,” said coach Rik Krumins. It was a big match for juniors George Stein and Peter Krumins, who recorded five goals and four goals respectively. “Peter was hitting shots from the outside and a lot of those were going in. George is an all-around player. He was scoring inside, scoring on 6-on-5 chances, and scoring on the counter attack. George was doing it all. It was a good game for him,” said coach Krumins. No. 3 Piedmont faces the second-ranked Wildcats of Marin Academy tomorrow, a rematch from the 2021 NCS Semifinals. The Highlanders will have the opportunity to avenge last year’s 7-4 postseason loss. “We know they are a really good team,” said Krumins. “Their players play on clubs yearround. We also know they are a good team of swimmers, and they are a team who has been at this level before. We expect them to be very confident and wellcoached. We have to bring our best to advance into the championship round. “We are confident and excited. If we execute our game plan, then I think we have a pretty good shot,” he said. “I think last year’s game is somewhat in the minds of our players, but it’s a different team for us and for them. They’ve lost some key seniors, and we lost three key seniors. We are a more balanced team than last year and we’re able to handle the counter attack, I think the boys are pretty confident going in,” Krumins added. PHS will face Marin Academy goalie Ezra Trost-Goldhammer, who is a Piedmont resident and competed in the Junior Olympics with club-team CC United alongside other PHS students. “They have a really good goalie who is actually from Piedmont. A lot of the players know each other from clubs, it’s going to be a good game,” said Krumins. Semifinals recap After conceding the opening goal of the game after 38 seconds, Piedmont gained a man-advantage at 6:05, leading to Stein scoring 13 seconds later. Novato scored again at the 5:24 mark, but it was the last time the Hornets held the lead. Daniel Banin made it 4-2 with 38 seconds left in the first. In the second quarter, Novato narrowed the gap to 4-3 after 40 seconds of action, but Piedmont responded after drawing a penalty at the 4:08 mark and Declan Linnane scoring 13 seconds later. Finn Burke added another for PHS with 1:47 left in the half, 6-3, and then #2 scored with another man-advantage. Novato tacked one on with 32 seconds left to make it 7-4 going into the half. articles.text: JV team ends season with 41-8 rout of Kennedy Piedmont High’s junior varsity football team closed its season on a high note by defeating Kennedy 41-8 on Thursday, November 3 at Witter Field. It was their third consecutive blowout win. Coach Jordan Seiden reflected on the season, pointing out that this is the energy they need to bring into their offseason program. Although Thursday’s game marked the season-finale for football, it seemed to represent the start of a new era of football in Piedmont. In the final three games of the season, the JV team outscored opponents 126-20. “These are the kids that are going to be the foundation of the program. We have some great building-blocks with a strong group of freshmen, sophomores, and juniors. They are all leadership-type kids at each level. This is a unique group, it’s exciting to be a part of,” said coach Seiden. Prior to the game, PHS honored its nine seniors on the varsity roster after having their season canceled after playing only four games. The players graduating are Bailey Cain, Ryan McConathy, Bautista and Matteo Costa, Marcos Filho, Aiden Hickman, Jack Nelson, Liam Campbell, and Luka Rivas Cate. Seiden was the head coach of the varsity team prior to its closure and then stepped to the JV team after the school decided to terminate the varsity season. Seiden has seen considerable progress from several players, giving high praise to tight end Albert Bellingrath, lineman Adrian Kondakov, running back and linebacker Tommy Ashton, and receiver and defensive back Marius Arno. “The thing we preach about football is about developing. Football is a developmental sport where you start at a baseline and grow from there. We spent a lot of time in the summer and preseason working out together and I got to know a lot of them, but then when you see the light bulb go on, it’s exciting. Albert never played tight end before and has been so excited to learn that spot. Tommy hadn’t played much running back until coming down to JV, now we’re looking at him being a feature back. Adrian is another kid who never played football and is a world-class chess champion. His development to starting both ways makes us view him as a staple. Marius is a player I talked to directly and his growth has been amazing,” said Seiden. Players like quarterback MarStaff Photos Quarterback Markos Lagios gets ready for a snap with Tommy Ashton behind him at running back. Receiver Sam Shelby scored three touchdowns against Kennedy. Photo by Chuck Wolf cos Lagios and Ashton got time at the varsity level and were able to see the speed from top-level teams like Del Norte and St. Mary’s. Their message to players who did not gain varsity experience is to play with confidence, don’t over complicate things, and take what’s in front of you. “This is really our future right here. It was good to get time together and build chemistry with everyone. I really think that adjusting to varsity is dealing with bigger players, the lights, and more pressure, but it’s really the same game. The advice I’d give is to treat it like every game, don’t overthink it, and stay relaxed,” said Lagios. “It was a tough season but we really came together and gained some momentum. I’d tell players that the pressure can get to you sometimes, but keep fighting and you’ll be fine. Play your best and always give your best effort,” added Ashton. Game Recap Piedmont started the game by recovering an onside kick and scored after just two plays including a 40-yard catch and run by receiver Sam Shelby—which was the first of three scores by the sophomore. PHS led 6-0 after a missed extra point at 8:34 in the first quarter. From there, Piedmont recovered a fumble at the Kennedy 48 yard line and scored after four plays on a 17-yard touchdown run by Ashton, who punched across a two-point conversion, 14-0, at 3:24. After a Kennedy punt to the PHS 44 yard line, the Highlanders capped off a seven play drive with a seven yard run by Ashton—an extra point made it 21-0 with 6:45 left in the first half. On the Eagles’ next series, they drove to the Piedmont 28 but failed to convert a fourth-andfour when Vince Arbit broke up a pass. The Highlanders drove six plays for the score on a 45-yard pass to Shelby—making it 28-0 with six seconds left. In the third, PHS scored with Ashton’s third touchdown, which was a 25-yard run to make it 34-0 after a missed extra point at 7:19. In the fourth, Kennedy finally got on the board with a long touchdown run with 9:34 left in the game—34-8. But on the ensuing kickoff, Shelby took the return to the house for the game’s final score, 41-8 with 7:59 to play. Piedmont honored its nine seniors from the varsity roster prior to Thursday’s game. Pictured are Aidan Hickman (75), Ryan McConathy (11), Marcos Filho (back), Jack Nelson (10), Bailey Cain, Liam Campbell, Bautista Costa, Matteo Costa (back), and Luka Rivas Cate.

articles.text: Staff Photos Trinity Zamora announces that she’ll continue playing basketball at San Diego State, a Div. 1 program. Piedmont senior Trinity Zamora, the basketball team’s leading scorer, intends to attend San Diego State and play for its Div. 1 team. Piedmont High School is hosting a ceremony today, November 9, for the senior to sign her Letter of Intent for her selected college team. “I think what drew me to the school the most was the coaches, the staff, and the team itself. It was very much like a family and San Diego is a place I could see myself living for a while, growing, and becoming a woman,” said Zamora. Zamora is a four-year starter at Piedmont High. In addition to her Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year as a junior, we named her our 2021 Sophomore of the Year and 2020 Freshman of the Year. She’ll undoubtedly be a front runner for 2023 Athlete of the Year honors. “We are so proud of Trinity; she is everything you want in a basketball player and leader,” said veteran Piedmont High coach Bryan Gardere. Zamora said she has felt a strong connection to the Aztecs’ coaching staff for two years, including head coach Stacie Terry-Hutson. “They’ve watched me play AAU and high school ball, and we connected very well. I’ve always been able to have good, comfortable conversations with them. It just felt like home; whenever I talked to them it felt like I was speaking to a family member. I really appreciate that about the school,” said Zamora. After making an official visit to the school, Zamora felt like the college and its facilities fulfilled her immediate dreams. “I took an official visit, and it’s beautiful. The campus is beautiful and it’s pretty big. Their gym is amazing; the practice facilities and locker rooms are nice. It’s just a beautiful facility allaround. And there’s a bunch of beaches in San Diego, of course,” she said with a laugh. Zamora said she also considered schools like Nevada, Sacramento State, and Loyola Marymount, but San Diego had many factors that drew her to Southern California. “Nevada and San Diego State were really my top-two. I’d say the facilities and the coaching set San Diego State apart. I could just see myself there compared to the other schools. San Diego just felt like home,” said Zamora. She is planning on exploring San Diego State’s Fowler College of Business. With the high school basketball season soon to begin, Zamora and her teammates are setting lofty goals. The starting five is likely to include AllLeague Natalia Martinez, Maddie Hill, Perseas Gioukaris, and Eva Levingston. The Highlanders fell narrowly short of winning their first WACC title since joining the league 11 years ago, yet they advanced in State post-season competition. “Our number one goal is to win state. We want to keep a strong record and go out with a bang. We have a lot of seniors and some transfer students from last season (Gioukaris and Levingston) who didn’t get to play. There is certainly a lot of built up tension ready to let off,” said Zamora. Other student-athletes who are announcing their college intent, please reach out to The Post at News@PiedmontPost.org and JonathanCX525@gmail.com to keep us informed. Trinity Zamora was the Post’s 2022 Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year, its Sophomore of the Year and 2021, and Freshman of the Year the year prior.

Turning around from this point will end your day at slightly over three miles of hiking. Hikers wanting to continue for an added workout, can walk uphill to Redwood Peak, where you will see a collection of boulders with initials and dates etched into their surface. It is a great location to relax and hydrate while you scour the boulders to find the oldest date. The oldest year I was able to find was more than 100 years ago, in 1918. To reach Redwood Peak, travel an additional half-mile to the Tres Sendas Trail, which will intersect with the Starflower Trail. Continue on the Starflower Trail for nearly a half-mile until you reach the Madrone Trail, taking the route on the right. You’ll venture on the Madrone Trail for nearly a half-mile until it becomes the Redwood Peak Trail, walking straight for .2 of a mile until reaching the boulders at the trail’s end. The venture from the Stream Trail to Redwood Peak will add 1,000 feet of elevation gain to your day. To return to your car, take the West Ridge Trail from Redwood Peak for 1.1 miles until reaching the Chown Trail, which you will take for another mile as it descends back to the Stream Trail. The Chown Trail has five switchback turns as you descend and is much narrower than the other trails, but surrounds you in beautiful redwood trees and ferns. You’ll occasionally hear a woodpecker knocking around trees for food. Once you’re back on the Stream Trail, venture to the right and walk for another mile back to the trailhead. articles.text: Special treat for kids at the Symphony San Francisco Symphony will present Fantasia in Concert on Tuesday, November 22, with Tim Davies as guest conductor. This special performance showcases the Symphony performing the music scores from two of Walt Disney’s most beloved animated feature films, Fantasia (1940) and its sequel by the same name made in 2000. Disney’s 1940 film introduced young children to the orchestral sounds of strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion, much as did Peter and the Wolf by Sergei Prokofiev in 1936. The 1940 Disney animated film opens with scenes of members of an orchestra gathering against a blue background and tuning their instruments. Davies, the guest conductor, is an Australian orchestrator and composer for film, television, and the concert stage. He has conducted numerous well-known songs in Hollywood, including “Anna and Elsa” from Disney’s more recent blockbuster Frozen. This performance is appropriate for families and will begin at 7:30 p.m. at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco. articles.text: San Francisco Ballet’s holiday favorite, Nutcracker, opens December 8 at the War Memorial Opera House, with performances through December 27. This special production is set in San Francisco’s post-1906 earthquake era, with opening scenes featuring famous landmarks such as the Painted Ladies by Alamo Square. Nutcracker is the longest-running production in the company’s history. San Francisco Ballet performs the ballet every year and features “a kaleidoscope” of more than 150 dancers to tell the story of the Sugarplum Fairy. Artistic Director and principal choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s production is inspired by the city of San Francisco, accompanied by the Opera Orchestra performing the familiar music score by Tchaikovsky. A diverse array of instruments are played during performances, including the glockenspiel, triangle, suspended cymbal, crash cymbal, tambourine, snare drum, bass drum, castanets, tam tam, ratchet, and timpani -- all played by three musicians. The scenic design is by Michael Yeargan; costumes by Martin Pakledinaz; lighting design by James F. Ingalls, and projection design by Wendall K. Harrington. Nutcracker is appropriate for children aged five and older; no children under the age of three will be permitted. The ballet runs two hours with one intermission. Tickets are selling quickly for performances on Christmas Eve, December 24. The production will end on December 27. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/nutcracker-dec-2022/. Photo by Erik Tomasson San Francisco Ballet dancers perform in Helgi Tomasson’s production of Nutcracker.

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre reimagines Emily Brontë’s gothic masterpiece, Wuthering Heights, in a new play by Emma Rice, premiering on November 18. The 1847 novel tells the story of the Earnshaws and Lintons, two families living on the West Yorkshire moors, and the compelling relationship between the characters Catherine and Heathcliff. Heathcliff is rescued from the Liverpool docks as a young child, adopted by the Earnshaws and taken to live at Wuthering Heights. He strikes a friendship with Catherine Earnshaw and soon a fierce love ignites. Leah Brotherhead is cast as Catherine. Her theatre credits include Gulliver’s Travels (Unicorn Theatre), Lands (Bush Theatre/Summer Hall Edinburgh Fringe), Two Gentlemen of Verona (The Globe Theatre/ Liverpool Everyman), Wolf Hall and Bring Up the Bodies (RSC/ Aldwych Theatre/The Winter Gardens on Broadway), and As You Like It (Lamb Players). The male lead of Heathcliff will be performed by Liam Tamne, whose performances included The Prince of Egypt (Dominion Theatre), Bonnie and Clyde (Theatre Royal Drury Lane), The Light in the Piazza (Royal Festival Hall/ LA Opera), Spamilton (Menier Chocolate Factory), and Mack and Mabel Concert with LMTO (Hackney Empire). The New York Times called the reimagining “a feat of storytelling that wraps itself around the audience, pulling us into its silliness and sorrow.” Visit https://www.berkeleyrep. org/shows/wuthering-heights/ to obtain tickets.

articles.text: The punchline usually comes at the end. There is nothing like a walk-off home run in baseball, or a sudden knockout in boxing, or a field goal at the end of a championship football game. In this case, the punchline comes at the very beginning. We need music education… now more than ever. My attendance at a recent concert made me do some real soul-searching. The concert itself was a distressing affair. Knowing how to respond in a diplomatic way was equally distressing. The advance publicity of a highly touted ensemble was indeed impressive. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Still Mine is a sensitively made, superbly acted film, starring two veteran actors, James Cromwell and Genevieve Bujold, portraying Craig and Irene Morrison. They have been married for 61 years, and live on a family farm in rural St. Martins, New Brunswick, Canada Based on true events, Still Mine is in many ways an elegiac drama, a metaphor for mortality, and a nuanced love story, suffused with intimacy, and written and directed by Michael McGowan. It is that rare film in which elderly people are not all but invisible. As old age begins to define them, Irene and Craig slowly begin to realize that their twostory farmhouse is showing decades of wear. Irene, is also revealing signs of early dementia, growing ever more distracted, forgetful, and incautious. Falling twice, the second accident results in a broken hip and a hospital stay. Resisting the worried bickering of their middle-aged children regarding what to do with Irene (a retirement home?), Craig decides to build a smaller, single-story house on a nearby 200- acre plot of open land. He is a master craftsman, owns a bevy of tools, knows quality timber, and was schooled in carpentry by his shipwright father. He sees no problem with constructing a cottage on his own land; that is, until he soon learns that he must meet government codes and submit drawn plans as well as paying what he regards as an unnecessary, bureaucratic fee of $400. He is informed of these requirements by an obstinate, unsympathetic building inspector (Jonathan Potts) who eventually places a “Stop Work” order on Craig’s newly framed house. He is told in the harshest terms that to ignore the codes and fail to submit his plans amounts to breaking the law and could result in standing before a municipal judge or even going to jail. Irascible as always, laconic in the extreme, Craig continues to build. When one of his sons suggests that perhaps Craig is too old (87) for such a project, he points out that “age is an abstraction and not a straightjacket.” But what Craig gradually begins to understand is that when it comes to Irene, aging is not an abstraction; rather, time is of the essence as is finishing the cottage. Still Mine. Written and directed by Michael McGowan. Starring James Cromwell, Genevieve Bujold, Julie Stewart. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2013. Now streaming on Prime/ VUDU/Peacock. articles.text: Review by Chris Honore’ The question that often comes to mind when watching a film such as Run All Night is, who is the audience? Films of this genre – call them pulp cinema – are dark and gritty and usually edged with nihilism. Run was shot in the boroughs of New York City and takes place over some 16 hours with hardcore shoot-outs and one prolonged chase scene on Jamaica Avenue in Queens that will take your breath away for all the destruction of public and private property involved. At the center of Run is Jimmy Conlon (Liam Neeson), a once mobbed-up hit man who was so good at what he did he was nicknamed “the gravedigger.” Over the years, his life has evolved into a train wreck and he’s finding it hard to live with his past and the price he has paid in terms of family, especially his estranged son, Mike (Joel Kinnaman), who has a lovely wife and two daughters. Profoundly alone, broke, and as much a part of the detritus of the streets as the isolated homeless huddled under blue plastic tarps, Jimmy lives off the generosity of Shawn Maguire (Ed Harris), the ex-gangster he once worked for, who is also his boyhood friend. They share a bond and repeatedly swear to cross the final finish line together. Of course, relying on that familiar line from Neeson’s Taken (a movie worth finding), Jimmy still has skill sets. In other words, he’s a blunt instrument. And for reasons far more complicated than is possible to detail here, his son, a limo driver suddenly, violently, finds himself in need of the father he has angrily pushed away. As circumstances would have it, Jimmy shoots a young man before he can shoot his son. Tragically, he is the only son of Shawn, Danny (Boyd Holbrook), who is into some very bad drug dealings with an Albanian cartel. Apparently, the Albanians are the new Sicilians. Shawn pledges that the only thing that will balance the scales is if he, or one of his hired thugs, kills Mike. Nothing Jimmy can say to Shawn will dissuade him. All he can promise is that he will do all within his power to stop Shawn and his men (one in particular, portrayed by Common). As a result, lots of people die badly. Which takes us back to the question regarding the audience. There is a solid fan base for these B-movies. Even when they feature middle aged actors who still have their mojo. Run All Night is well done and for the intended moviegoers who find these stylized, urban movies engaging, they will not be disappointed. The film is intense, a game clock of sorts is ticking, and time is telescoped into one night that happens to be Christmas Eve (the irony is not lost). Action-thriller? Definitely. Is it a cliché? Indeed. But in the best sense of the word. Run All Night. Directed by Juame Collet-Serra. Starring Liam Neeson, Ed Harris and Joel Kinnaman. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated R. Released in 2015, Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

At the center of Run is Jimmy Conlon (Liam Neeson), a once mobbed-up hit man who was so good at what he did he was nicknamed “the gravedigger.” Over the years, his life has evolved into a train wreck and he’s finding it hard to live with his past and the price he has paid in terms of family, especially his estranged son, Mike (Joel Kinnaman), who has a lovely wife and two daughters. Profoundly alone, broke, and as much a part of the detritus of the streets as the isolated homeless huddled under blue plastic tarps, Jimmy lives off the generosity of Shawn Maguire (Ed Harris), the ex-gangster he once worked for, who is also his boyhood friend. They share a bond and repeatedly swear to cross the final finish line together. Of course, relying on that familiar line from Neeson’s Taken (a movie worth finding), Jimmy still has skill sets. In other words, he’s a blunt instrument. And for reasons far more complicated than is possible to detail here, his son, a limo driver suddenly, violently, finds himself in need of the father he has angrily pushed away. As circumstances would have it, Jimmy shoots a young man before he can shoot his son. Tragically, he is the only son of Shawn, Danny (Boyd Holbrook), who is into some very bad drug dealings with an Albanian cartel. Apparently, the Albanians are the new Sicilians. Shawn pledges that the only thing that will balance the scales is if he, or one of his hired thugs, kills Mike. Nothing Jimmy can say to Shawn will dissuade him. All he can promise is that he will do all within his power to stop Shawn and his men (one in particular, portrayed by Common). As a result, lots of people die badly. Which takes us back to the question regarding the audience. There is a solid fan base for these B-movies. Even when they feature middle aged actors who still have their mojo. Run All Night is well done and for the intended moviegoers who find these stylized, urban movies engaging, they will not be disappointed. The film is intense, a game clock of sorts is ticking, and time is telescoped into one night that happens to be Christmas Eve (the irony is not lost). Action-thriller? Definitely. Is it a cliché? Indeed. But in the best sense of the word. Run All Night. Directed by Juame Collet-Serra. Starring Liam Neeson, Ed Harris and Joel Kinnaman. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated R. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Freaky Friday is a family-friendly comedy, ideal for kids (8+), tweens and teens, but not to forget that parents will find lots to smile at as well. At the center of the story is single mom Tess (Jamie Lee Curtis), widowed several years ago and now on the brink of marrying Ryan (Mark Harmon). Her daughter, Anna (Lindsay Lohan), just 15, is a surly teenager. The two frequently find themselves at odds. Actually, they couldn’t be more different. Tess is a multi-tasking, stressed-out psychologist, who is either on her cell phone, checking her Palm Pilot, or seeing patients. Anna plays the guitar, is failing English, generally feckless and often in detention. One evening they go out for a Chinese dinner, the meal followed by a fortune cookie. While all seems benign, we soon learn that it wasn’t. Inexplicably, they wake up the next morning having discovered that they have, in effect, well, body-swapped. While it isn’t a new premise, as films go in Hollywood (recall Big with Tom Hanks, for example), Lohan and Curtis do a superb job trying to adjust to this remarkable change. Both stand before the mirror and have that expected “Good grief, what’s happened to me?” moment. Both actors are having fun with their roles, conveying that Jamie Lee Curtis and Lindsay Lohan in Freaky Friday. neither is prepared to walk in the other’s shoes. Tess can’t play the guitar, nor can she do algebra, nor navigate school. Anna stumbles through Tees’ neurotic patient appointments, and even attends a talk show where she tries to sell her mom’s recently published book on aging. Tess has a hilarious problem when she is confronted with the very awkward attention of Anna’s hunky, motorcycle riding boyfriend, Jake (Chad Michael Murray) who doesn’t want to take “no” for an answer. All of this amounts to one hilarious moment after the next, using the fulcrum word “empathy”l while the story unfolds. Though they were both in constant disagreement, slowly they develop lots of insights into one another. Anna comes to understand what it means to be a mom, and her mom realizes that being a teen is no walk in the park, what with all the changes in moods that define what it means to be an adolescent. Reconciliation is not far off. Freaky Friday. Directed by Mark Waters. Starring Jamie Lee Curtis, Lindsay Lohan, Mark Harmon. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG. Released in 2003. articles.text: Part 56 in a bi-weekly series Croatia’s Dubrovnik, the Dalmatian Coast city dubbed “the pearl of the Adriatic”, is an incredible place. It was included early at the start of the UNESCO World Heritage Listings in 1979. The old city is filled with a beautiful range of different architectural styles appropriate to the local tradition and geography – the very definition of the word “eclectic”. Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque buildings give it a wonderful rich and interesting visual texture. But the totality of the place, the designed combination of buildings, streets, courtyards, plazas, pathways, light fixtures, landscaping and paving, in short, the Urban Design, is what ultimately make it the place it is. Contributing greatly to this specialness is its pedestrian function and character. The entire walled Old Town is a car-free zone! What also is endearing to me about Dubrovnik has to do with why I write this column: encouraging people to become educated relative to our built environment, and as a result to care about it. In 1991 during the Croatian war of independence, an ISIS-like bombardment of the Old Town during the Siege of Dubrovnik provoked immediate international outrage and condemnation over the senseless destruction of the priceless cultural heritage. The following diplomatic and economic reaction actually changed the course of the war. It is encouraging to recall that many people do care – many a great deal. Ljubljana Slovenia, Croatia’s Balkan neighbor to the north with its relatively small (p 280,000) yet remarkable capital city of Ljubljana (loo blee ah nuh), is another wonderful gem of urban design and pedestrian accommodation. The work of architect Joze Plecnik, was instrumental in forming the identity of this place. Though famous in that part of the world, I had never heard of him until visiting recently and discovering the extent of his legacy. His work has been described as “human centered urban design”. It resonates strongly with me, respecting the history and geography of the place while accommodating modern programing needs; respecting, but not a slave to historical styles. In 2012 in order to reverse a continuous increase in automobile use clogging the center of town, Ljubljana adopted a plan to limit personal motor vehicle traffic and instead give priority Photos & sketches by Will Adams Dubrovnik Croatia: the density, eclectic architectural character, and urban design of this strictly pedestrian town make it an incredible place. So much so, that dealing with “over-tourism” (like in Venice just across the Adriatic) is its biggest problem. That aside, there is much we can learn from the many-faceted richness of this place.

articles.text: If you receive Social Security, you’ve probably already heard that your checks in 2023 will be bigger – considerably bigger, in fact. How can you make the best use of this extra money? Here’s what’s happening: For 2023, there’s an 8.7% cost-ofliving adjustment (COLA) for Social Security benefits – the largest increase in 40 years. Also, the monthly Medicare Part B premiums are declining next year, to $164.90/month from $170.10/ month, which will also modestly boost Social Security checks for those enrolled in Part B, as these premiums are automatically deducted. Of course, the sizable COLA is due to the high inflation of 2022, as the Social Security Administration uses a formula based on increases in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). So, it’s certainly possible that you will need some, or perhaps all, of your larger checks to pay for the increased cost of goods and services. But if your cash flow is already relatively strong, you might want to consider these suggestions for using your bigger checks: • Reduce withdrawals from your investment portfolio. When you’re retired, you will likely need to withdraw a certain amount from your portfolio each year to meet your expenses. A boost in your Social Security may enable you to withdraw less, at least for a year. This can be particularly advantageous when the markets are down, as you’d like to avoid, as much as possible, selling investments and withdrawing the money when investment prices are low. And the fewer investments you need to sell, the longer your portfolio may last during your retirement years. • Help build your cash reserves. When you’re retired, it’s a good idea to maintain about a year’s worth of the amount you’ll spend from your portfolio in cash, while also keeping three months’ of your spending needs in an emergency fund, with the money kept in a liquid, low-risk account. Your higher Social Security checks could help you build these cash reserves. (Also, it’s helpful to keep another three to five years’ worth of spending from your portfolio in short-term, fixed-income investments, which now, due to higher interest rates, offer better income opportunities.) • Contribute to a 529 plan. You could use some of your extra Social Security money to contribute to a tax-advantaged 529 education savings plan for your grandchildren or other family members. • Contribute to charitable organizations. You might want to use some of your Social Security money to expand your charitable giving. Your generosity will help worthy groups and possibly bring you some tax benefits, too. While it’s nice to have these possible options in 2023, you can’t count on future COLA increases being as large. The jump in inflation in 2022 was due to several unusual factors, including pandemic-related government spending, supply shortages and the Russian invasion of Ukraine. It’s quite possible, perhaps even likely, that inflation will subside in 2023, which, in turn, would mean a smaller COLA bump in 2024. Nonetheless, while you might not want to include large annual COLA increases as part of your long-term financial strategy, you may well choose to take advantage, in some of the ways described above, of the bigger Social Security checks you’ll receive in 2023. When opportunity knocks, you may want to open the door. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. Edward Jones, Member SIPC. T.J. articles.text: It’s Saturday afternoon, and I am enjoying all the things about my home that I try to create for my clients. It feels welcoming and quiet, orderly and beautiful, and it’s the perfect place to be after two weeks of traveling abroad to Switzerland and Cape Town, South Africa. I feel grateful not only for shelter, but for one that welcomed me home with such a feeling of lightness and comfort. It feels like me. I love it for how it has supported me throughout my darkest days and my happiest moments, as we have raised a family and grown a business. It is a place where a stranger can feel welcome and be invited to go deep. When I think about it, my home has evolved along with me, and has supported me on my journey to becoming the version I am now. Before I left on the trip, I asked Gray Cathrall for a reprieve from writing my column in the Post, A Life By Design, for a month. I wanted to make sure my clients and staff had what they needed before my departure. I intended to create space to get things done in advance of my trip. But the moment I made the request, I realized what I really needed was more space for new creative endeavors to germinate. Life is asking for something novel and different for me right now, and I’m feeling called to pivot toward some of the other projects that fuel my multi-passionate self. I have a desire to let go of some things to make room for what’s next. I don’t know exactly what it is, but life has taught me to get still so I can hear it speak. Even though this is my last column for the Piedmont Post, it’s not a goodbye. LMB Interiors is thriving, and my intention is that it keeps evolving, serving, and connecting to this community. When I asked Gray if I could write a column for the Piedmont Post seven years ago, I had no idea it would become such a fulfilling experience. Through the years, I have made new friends through this outlet. I’ve crossed paths with incredible people who appreciate interior design as a way to create connection through heart-centered living. For those of you who have become regular readers over the years and have reached out to comment and share their insights, I am grateful. My intent has always been to take you on a My friend, the Klein Constantia bull. I hope you will continue to follow me on social media, and through my newsletter which you can sign up for on lmbinteriors.com. In the meantime, LMB Interiors will continue to serve the community through our design services, and by sourcing curated, local, artisan-crafted interiors that reflect the value of conscious consumerism and thoughtful details we have become known for.
